questions.question: Explain the difference between push and pull factors in rural–urban migration, giving two South African examples of each.
questions.expected_answer: Push factors are conditions in rural areas that drive people out — e.g. unemployment as commercial farms mechanise, poor services such as distant clinics and under-resourced schools, drought, and plots too small to subdivide. Pull factors are the real or believed attractions of cities — e.g. jobs and higher wages, better schools and hospitals, electricity and piped water, and family members who moved earlier. Migrants often move on perception of opportunity, which the city does not always deliver.

questions.question: Describe the consequences of rural depopulation for the people who remain and for the settlement itself.
questions.expected_answer: The age–sex structure hollows out: children, the elderly and often women remain while working-age adults leave, so the dependency ratio rises and households rely on grants and remittances; skills and leadership drain away. The place declines: fields go out of cultivation, buildings decay, schools, shops and services close for lack of numbers, feeding a downward spiral. Balanced answers note remittances flowing back, eased land pressure, and returning migrants bringing skills.

questions.question: Name and distinguish the three legs of South Africa's land reform programme.
questions.expected_answer: Tenure reform strengthens the rights of people already occupying land — protecting farm dwellers from eviction and formalising communal rights — without moving anyone. Redistribution transfers farmland to black South Africans for equity and livelihoods, forward-looking with no specific historical claim needed. Restitution returns specific land (or pays compensation) to people or communities dispossessed after 19 June 1913 by racially discriminatory laws.
